title: Policy Writing
text:
Policy memo to the House Task Force on Artificial Intelligence · March 2026
Police use of facial recognition is growing with almost no federal regulation. This memo reviews how the technology works and how law enforcement uses it. It covers the evidence on accuracy and demographic error gaps, and the lack of disclosure to defendants. It then assesses H.R. 4695 and recommends amendments on algorithmic bias, developer accountability and federal oversight. The memo draws on 22 sources, including NIST and GAO reports.






Written for a university public policy course. The assignment was to write on behalf of an advocacy organisation of my own design, so The Privacy Project is fictional and is not a real organisation or employer.

title: Cabinet Churn and Democratic Erosion
text: Do autocrats reshuffle their cabinets to stop rivals building power bases (“coup-proofing”)? And do purges come before or after spikes in executive authoritarian events?

title: Cabinet Churn and Democratic Erosion
text: Do autocrats reshuffle their cabinets to stop rivals building power bases (“coup-proofing”)? And do purges come before or after spikes in executive authoritarian events?

title: Cabinet Churn and Democratic Erosion
text:
Key findings

No coup-proofing signal yet: autocracies replace 30.4% of ministers a year and democracies 35.3%, probably because elections replace whole cabinets.
Turnover doesn’t clearly move around spikes: the post-spike effect is 0.028 (SE 0.038).
Polyarchy was already falling before spikes, so spikes look like part of an existing slide rather than its start.

title: Research
text:
Emily McKay · Faculty mentor: Prof. Maria Popova · American University, 2026






Session winner, “Justice, Equality, & Power,” 18th Annual Undergraduate Research Symposium, American University, April 2026.



Democratic backsliding is usually pinned on strongmen. This paper asks which institutions’ authoritarian actions actually predict democratic decline. I merged 23,421 hand-coded events from the Democratic Erosion Event Dataset with V-Dem democracy scores. Then I used two-part fixed-effects panel models to separate the onset of authoritarian behaviour by an institution from its escalation.
Main findings: the military, police, judiciary and ruling party each predict decline independently of the head of state. The first authoritarian action by a new institution is a stronger warning sign than further actions by one already involved. Sustained civil-society and international engagement are associated with resilience.
Read the paper (PDF) Symposium slides (PDF) Project page Code


Spatial contagion of democratic backsliding. Do authoritarian events in neighbouring countries predict later democratic decline at home? This extension uses a contiguity-weighted spatial lag of DEED events and draws on theories of demonstration effects.

title: How Close Are the World’s Parties?
text: Do parties cluster by country or by ideology? I compared 226 parties that won at least 5% of the vote, in two ways: by their manifesto wording and by the Manifesto Project’s hand-coded policy categories.

title: How Close Are the World’s Parties?
text: Do parties cluster by country or by ideology? I compared 226 parties that won at least 5% of the vote, in two ways: by their manifesto wording and by the Manifesto Project’s hand-coded policy categories.

title: How Close Are the World’s Parties?
text:
Key findings

Wording clusters by country. Parties in the same country use similar words, even across party families.
Policy clusters by party family. Greens and the left group together, and so does the radical right. Germany’s AfD is closest to Switzerland’s SVP, the Netherlands’ FvD and Spain’s VOX.
After correcting for document length, the two measures agree at a correlation of 0.46.

title: About Me
text:
I’m a Data Science for Political Science undergraduate at American University, spending 2026–27 on the General Course at the London School of Economics. I’m interested in how institutions erode or protect democracy, and in using data to make that kind of question answerable.
My favourite projects start with a question that’s hard to measure. I build the dataset from scratch, test whether the result holds up, and then explain it clearly. My research on which institutions drive democratic backsliding won its session at American University’s 2026 Undergraduate Research Symposium.
I’m looking for policy research, data analysis and research-assistant roles where cross-national data and careful methods inform real decisions.
